title: Tangents to a Circle: Secant vs Tangent Limits & Theorem 10.1 Perpendicularity Proof
description: Understand the geometric definition of a tangent to a circle as a limiting case of a secant when the two intersection points coincide. Rigorously prove Theorem 10.1: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact, using the shortest distance property.
key_concepts: Secant: A straight line that intersects a circle in two distinct points
Tangent: A straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point (Point of Contact)
Limiting Case: A tangent is the limiting position of a secant when its two end-points of intersection coincide
Theorem 10.1: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact

Shortest Distance Principle: The shortest distance from an external point to a straight line is the perpendicular distance; any point Q on the tangent line other than P lies strictly outside the circle, hence OQ > OP
subtopics: Differentiating non-intersecting lines, secants, and tangents
Full formal proof of Theorem 10.1 by contradiction / shortest distance
Number of tangents from points inside, on, and outside a circle

worked_examples.solution:
STATEMENT: Prove that the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.

GIVEN:
A circle C(O, r) with centre O and a tangent XY touching the circle at point P.
OP is the radius through the point of contact P.

TO PROVE:
OP ⊥ XY.

CONSTRUCTION:
Take any point Q on the tangent line XY other than P. Join OQ. Let OQ intersect the circle at point R.

PROOF:
Step 1: Determine position of Q relative to the circle:
Since XY is a tangent to the circle at point P, P is the only point on the line XY that lies on the circle.
Every other point on the line XY must lie strictly outside the circle.
Therefore, point Q lies outside the circle.

Step 2: Compare lengths OQ and OP:
Since point R lies on the circle and between O and Q:
OQ = OR + RQ
Since OR = OP (radii of the same circle):
OQ = OP + RQ
Since RQ > 0:
OQ > OP.

Step 3: Conclude shortest distance:
This inequality OQ > OP holds true for EVERY point Q on the line XY, except the point of contact P.
Therefore, the line segment OP is the shortest of all the distances of the point O to the points on the line XY.
We know from Euclidean geometry that the shortest distance between a point and a line is the perpendicular distance.

Therefore, OP ⊥ XY.
Hence Proved!
[ROUGH_WORK]
Shortest distance from point O to line XY is perpendicular. Since OP is radius and every other point on line is outside the circle, OP is strictly minimum!
Boxed Answer: [ OP ⊥ XY (Proved) ].
concept_questions: Why must point Q lie outside the circle?
What would happen if Q lay inside the circle?

common_misconceptions: Thinking a circle can have parallel tangents at adjacent points: A circle can only have parallel tangents at the diametrically opposite endpoints of a diameter!
Believing a tangent crosses inside the circle: By definition, a tangent touches the circle at exactly one point without entering the interior.

title: Tangents from an External Point: Theorem 10.2 Proof (PA = PB) & Angle Subtensions
description: Rigorously prove Theorem 10.2: The lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal. Master the two fundamental corollaries: (1) tangents subtend equal angles at the centre (∠AOP = ∠BOP), and (2) tangents are equally inclined to the line joining the point to the centre (∠APO = ∠BPO).
key_concepts: Theorem 10.2: The lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal (PA = PB)
RHS Congruence Proof: Hypotenuse OP is common; Radii OA = OB; Right angles ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90° (by Theorem 10.1)
Central Angle Bisector: OP bisects ∠AOB (∠AOP = ∠BOP)
External Angle Bisector: OP bisects ∠APB (∠APO = ∠BPO)

Supplementary Angle Theorem: The angle between the two tangents (∠APB) and the angle subtended by the line segment joining the points of contact at the centre (∠AOB) are supplementary: ∠APB + ∠AOB = 180°
subtopics: Formal statement and proof of Theorem 10.2

worked_examples.problem: Theorem 10.2 (NCERT): Prove that the lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.
worked_examples.solution:
STATEMENT: The lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.

GIVEN:
A circle with centre O, an external point P, and two tangents PA and PB drawn from P to the circle, touching at A and B respectively.

TO PROVE:
PA = PB.

CONSTRUCTION:
Join OA, OB, and OP.

PROOF:
In triangles ΔOAP and ΔOBP:
1. ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90° (By Theorem 10.1: Radius through point of contact is perpendicular to tangent)
2. OP = OP (Common hypotenuse)
3. OA = OB (Radii of the same circle)

Therefore, by RHS (Right angle - Hypotenuse - Side) Congruence Criterion:
ΔOAP ≅ ΔOBP.

Since corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal (CPCT):
PA = PB.

Corollaries from CPCT:
(i) ∠OPA = ∠OPB (OP is the angle bisector of ∠APB)
(ii) ∠AOP = ∠BOP (OP is the angle bisector of ∠AOB)
Hence Proved!
[ROUGH_WORK]
Alternative proof using Pythagoras Theorem:
PA² = OP² - OA² = OP² - r²
PB² = OP² - OB² = OP² - r²
⇒ PA² = PB² ⇒ PA = PB (since lengths > 0).
Boxed Answer: [ PA = PB (Proved) ].

worked_examples.problem: Example 2 (NCERT): Two tangents TP and TQ are drawn to a circle with centre O from an external point T. Prove that ∠PTQ = 2 ∠OPQ.
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
A circle with centre O, an external point T, and tangents TP and TQ touching the circle at P and Q.

TO PROVE:
∠PTQ = 2 ∠OPQ.

PROOF:
Let ∠PTQ = θ.

Step 1: Analyze ΔTPQ:
By Theorem 10.2, the lengths of tangents from an external point T are equal:
TP = TQ.
Therefore, ΔTPQ is an isosceles triangle with TP = TQ.
In an isosceles triangle, angles opposite to equal sides are equal:
∠TPQ = ∠TQP.

Step 2: Use Angle Sum Property in ΔTPQ:
∠PTQ + ∠TPQ + ∠TQP = 180°
θ + 2 ∠TPQ = 180°
2 ∠TPQ = 180° - θ
∠TPQ = (180° - θ) / 2 = 90° - θ/2 ... (1)

Step 3: Relate to radius OP:
By Theorem 10.1, the radius OP is perpendicular to the tangent TP at point P:
∠OPT = 90°.
Notice that ∠OPT = ∠OPQ + ∠TPQ:
∠OPQ + ∠TPQ = 90°
∠OPQ = 90° - ∠TPQ

Step 4: Substitute ∠TPQ from equation (1):
∠OPQ = 90° - (90° - θ/2)
∠OPQ = 90° - 90° + θ/2
∠OPQ = θ / 2
Multiply both sides by 2:
2 ∠OPQ = θ
Since θ = ∠PTQ:
∠PTQ = 2 ∠OPQ.
Hence Proved!
[ROUGH_WORK]
Key insight: In isosceles ΔTPQ, base angle is 90° - θ/2. Since radius OP ⊥ TP (90°), the remaining angle ∠OPQ is exactly θ/2!
Boxed Answer: [ ∠PTQ = 2 ∠OPQ (Proved) ].

description: Complete step-by-step resolution of NCERT Exercise 10.1 (all 4 questions) and Exercise 10.2 Questions 1 through 5. worked_examples.problem: Exercise 10.2 Q4: Prove that the tangents drawn at the ends of a diameter of a circle are parallel.
worked_examples.solution:
STATEMENT: Tangents drawn at the ends of a diameter of a circle are parallel.

GIVEN:
A circle with centre O and diameter AB. Let line PQ be the tangent at end A, and line RS be the tangent at end B.

TO PROVE:
PQ || RS.

PROOF:
Step 1: Use Theorem 10.1 at point A:
Since AB is a diameter, OA is a radius.
PQ is the tangent to the circle at point of contact A.
By Theorem 10.1, the radius through the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent:
OA ⊥ PQ
Therefore, ∠PAB = 90° and ∠QAB = 90° ... (1)

Step 2: Use Theorem 10.1 at point B:
OB is the radius through the point of contact B.
RS is the tangent to the circle at point of contact B.
By Theorem 10.1, OB ⊥ RS:
Therefore, ∠ABR = 90° and ∠ABS = 90° ... (2)

Step 3: Compare alternate interior angles:
Notice the transversal line AB intersects line PQ and line RS.
From (1) and (2):
∠PAB = 90° and ∠ABS = 90°
⇒ ∠PAB = ∠ABS.
These are alternate interior angles formed by transversal AB with lines PQ and RS.

Since the alternate interior angles are equal, the lines must be parallel:
PQ || RS.
Hence Proved!
[ROUGH_WORK]
Alternatively, consecutive interior angles ∠PAB + ∠ABR = 90° + 90° = 180° (supplementary), proving PQ || RS directly!
Boxed Answer: [ PQ || RS (Proved) ].

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 10.2 Q8: A quadrilateral ABCD is drawn to circumscribe a circle. Prove that AB + CD = AD + BC.
worked_examples.solution:
STATEMENT: A quadrilateral ABCD is drawn to circumscribe a circle. Prove that AB + CD = AD + BC.

GIVEN:
A quadrilateral ABCD circumscribing a circle with centre O.
Let the sides AB, BC, CD, and DA touch the circle at points P, Q, R, and S respectively.

TO PROVE:
AB + CD = AD + BC.

PROOF:
By Theorem 10.2, the lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.
1. From external point A: AP = AS ... (1)
2. From external point B: BP = BQ ... (2)
3. From external point C: CR = CQ ... (3)
4. From external point D: DR = DS ... (4)

Step 1: Add equations (1), (2), (3), and (4) together:
(AP + BP) + (CR + DR) = (AS + DS) + (BQ + CQ)

Step 2: Group adjacent segments on each side of the quadrilateral:
Notice that:
AP + BP = AB
CR + DR = CD
AS + DS = AD
BQ + CQ = BC

Step 3: Substitute the grouped segments:
AB + CD = AD + BC.
Hence Proved!
[ROUGH_WORK]
Key rule: When writing the 4 tangent equality equations, make sure that segments belonging to the SAME side (like AP and BP) are placed on the SAME side of the equals sign!
Boxed Answer: [ AB + CD = AD + BC (Proved) ].
concept_questions: Why must AP and BP be on the same side of the equations before adding?
What special quadrilateral results if ABCD is a parallelogram?

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 10.2 Q9: In Fig., XY and X'Y' are two parallel tangents to a circle with centre O and another tangent AB with point of contact C intersecting XY at A and X'Y' at B. Prove that ∠AOB = 90°.
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
A circle with centre O. XY || X'Y' are tangents touching at P and Q respectively.
AB is another tangent with point of contact C, intersecting XY at A and X'Y' at B.

TO PROVE:
∠AOB = 90°.

CONSTRUCTION:
Join OC.

PROOF:
Step 1: Prove ΔOPA ≅ ΔOCA:
In ΔOPA and ΔOCA:
1. OP = OC (Radii of the same circle)
2. AP = AC (Tangents from external point A, Theorem 10.2)
3. OA = OA (Common side)
Therefore, by SSS Congruence Criterion:
ΔOPA ≅ ΔOCA.
By CPCT:
∠POA = ∠COA ... (1)
Therefore, ∠POC = 2 ∠COA.

Step 2: Prove ΔOQB ≅ ΔOCB:
Similarly, in ΔOQB and ΔOCB:
1. OQ = OC (Radii)
2. BQ = BC (Tangents from external point B)
3. OB = OB (Common)
Therefore, ΔOQB ≅ ΔOCB (by SSS).
By CPCT:
∠QOB = ∠COB ... (2)
Therefore, ∠QOC = 2 ∠COB.

Step 3: Use linear pair on diameter POQ:
Since XY || X'Y' and OP ⊥ XY, OQ ⊥ X'Y', POQ is a straight line diameter of the circle.
Therefore, the sum of angles on straight line POQ is 180°:
∠POC + ∠QOC = 180°
Substitute from (1) and (2):
2 ∠COA + 2 ∠COB = 180°
2 (∠COA + ∠COB) = 180°
∠COA + ∠COB = 180° / 2 = 90°
Notice that ∠COA + ∠COB = ∠AOB:
∠AOB = 90°.
Hence Proved!
[ROUGH_WORK]
2(∠1 + ∠2) = 180° ⇒ ∠1 + ∠2 = 90°. Classical board exam topper proof!
Boxed Answer: [ ∠AOB = 90° (Proved) ].

What congruence criterion was used to prove ΔOPA ≅ ΔOCA?

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 10.2 Q11: Prove that the parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus.
worked_examples.solution:
STATEMENT: Prove that the parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus.

GIVEN:
A parallelogram ABCD circumscribing a circle with centre O, touching the sides AB, BC, CD, and DA at P, Q, R, and S respectively.
Since ABCD is a parallelogram:
AB = CD ... (1) (Opposite sides of parallelogram are equal)
AD = BC ... (2)

TO PROVE:
ABCD is a rhombus (i.e. AB = BC = CD = DA).

PROOF:
Step 1: Apply Theorem 10.2 (Lengths of tangents from external points are equal):
From A: AP = AS
From B: BP = BQ
From C: CR = CQ
From D: DR = DS
Adding these 4 equations:
(AP + BP) + (CR + DR) = (AS + DS) + (BQ + CQ)
AB + CD = AD + BC ... (3) (As proved in Exercise 10.2 Q8)

Step 2: Substitute opposite sides of parallelogram from (1) and (2) into (3):
Replace CD with AB, and replace BC with AD:
AB + AB = AD + AD
2 AB = 2 AD
Divide both sides by 2:
AB = AD ... (4)

Step 3: Combine with parallelogram properties:
From (1), (2), and (4):
AB = BC = CD = DA.

Since ABCD is a parallelogram with all four sides equal in length, it is by definition a rhombus!
Hence Proved!
[ROUGH_WORK]
Parallelogram + Adjacent sides equal = Rhombus. Direct, 4-step clean deduction!
Boxed Answer: [ ABCD is a Rhombus (Proved) ].

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 10.2 Q12: A triangle ABC is drawn to circumscribe a circle of radius 4 cm such that the segments BD and DC into which BC is divided by the point of contact D are of lengths 8 cm and 6 cm respectively. Find the sides AB and AC.
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
ΔABC circumscribes a circle of radius r = OD = OE = OF = 4 cm.
Point D on BC divides it into BD = 8 cm and DC = 6 cm.
Therefore, BC = BD + DC = 8 + 6 = 14 cm.

Let the circle touch AC at E and AB at F.
By Theorem 10.2 (Tangents from an external point are equal):
From point C: CE = CD = 6 cm.
From point B: BF = BD = 8 cm.
From point A: Let AF = AE = x cm (where x > 0).

Side lengths of ΔABC:
a = BC = 14 cm
b = AC = AE + CE = x + 6 cm
c = AB = AF + BF = x + 8 cm.

Step 1: Calculate semi-perimeter 's' of ΔABC:
s = (a + b + c) / 2 = [ 14 + (x + 6) + (x + 8) ] / 2 = (2x + 28) / 2 = x + 14 cm.

Step 2: Compute Area of ΔABC using Heron's Formula:
s - a = (x + 14) - 14 = x
s - b = (x + 14) - (x + 6) = 8
s - c = (x + 14) - (x + 8) = 6
Area(ΔABC) = √[ s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c) ]
= √[ (x + 14)(x)(8)(6) ]
= √[ 48x (x + 14) ] ... (1)

Step 3: Compute Area of ΔABC as sum of 3 sub-triangles (ΔOBC, ΔOCA, ΔOAB):
Join OA, OB, OC. The radii OD, OE, OF are perpendicular heights (r = 4 cm) to the three sides:
Area(ΔOBC) = 1/2 × Base × Height = 1/2 × 14 × 4 = 28 cm²
Area(ΔOCA) = 1/2 × (x + 6) × 4 = 2(x + 6) = 2x + 12 cm²
Area(ΔOAB) = 1/2 × (x + 8) × 4 = 2(x + 8) = 2x + 16 cm²
Total Area = 28 + (2x + 12) + (2x + 16) = 4x + 56 = 4(x + 14) cm² ... (2)

Step 4: Equate the two area expressions:
√[ 48x (x + 14) ] = 4(x + 14)
Square both sides:
48x (x + 14) = 16 (x + 14)²
Since x + 14 > 0, divide both sides by 16(x + 14):
3x = x + 14
3x - x = 14
2x = 14 ⇒ x = 7 cm.

Step 5: Compute side lengths AB and AC:
AB = x + 8 = 7 + 8 = 15 cm.
AC = x + 6 = 7 + 6 = 13 cm.
[ROUGH_WORK]
Check Heron's area: s = 7 + 14 = 21. Area = √(21 × 7 × 8 × 6) = √(7056) = 84 cm².
Check 1/2 × r × Perimeter = 1/2 × 4 × 42 = 84 cm² (Verified!).
Boxed Answer: [ AB = 15 cm, AC = 13 cm ].
